title: Mencius’s Four Sprouts — moral potential needs cultivation
when: Mencius was active in China’s Warring States period, probably in the fourth century BCE; traditional dates are c. 372–289 BCE, though some scholars place his birth earlier. The Mengzi was likely compiled by his disciples or their successors.
people: Mencius (Meng Ke); Confucius as his intellectual predecessor; later interpreters including Zhu Xi.
origin: Confucian philosophy in northeastern China during the Warring States era, when thinkers debated how to restore ethical and political order.
idea: Mencius argues that people possess incipient tendencies toward virtue, which he calls the “four sprouts.” Compassion is the beginning of benevolence; shame and dislike, of righteousness; deference, of ritual propriety; and approval and disapproval, of wisdom. His famous example is the alarm anyone would feel on seeing a child about to fall into a well: an immediate response that is not yet a fully developed virtue, but can be extended and cultivated. The agricultural metaphor matters: sprouts are neither finished moral achievements nor guarantees of goodness. They need nourishment through reflection, education, relationships, and humane social conditions; neglect or adverse circumstances can stunt them. Mencius’s view is therefore more nuanced than the slogan that people are simply “born good.” It presents moral development as the shaping of natural emotional capacities into reliable judgment and action.
relevance: The sprouts suggest that ethical education can begin from ordinary human responses, while also reminding us that good intentions are not enough. Families, schools, and institutions can either help people extend compassion and fairness or make those capacities harder to exercise. The view invites a practical question: what conditions help our best impulses mature?
